lesson.title: Everyone's War: Mobilizing Industry, Food, and Money at Home
lesson.summary: Fighting a modern industrial war required organizing the entire American economy, prompting new federal agencies to direct factories, conserve food, and finance the effort, changes that reshaped American society far beyond the millions of men drafted under the Selective Service Act.
lesson.body:
Raising and equipping the large army described in the previous chapter was only part of the challenge. The United States also had to reorganize its economy to supply that army with weapons, uniforms, food, and transportation, all while continuing to support Britain and France. The federal government responded by creating a series of powerful new wartime agencies that reached into nearly every corner of American life.

The War Industries Board, led from 1918 by the financier Bernard Baruch, coordinated industrial production across the country, allocating scarce raw materials, standardizing manufacturing processes, and effectively planning large portions of the economy to maximize war output. The Food Administration, headed by future president Herbert Hoover, took a different approach, relying on voluntary conservation rather than legally mandated rationing. Hoover's agency popularized campaigns like Meatless Mondays and Wheatless Wednesdays and encouraged families to plant so-called war gardens, all so that more food could be shipped overseas to feed American troops and hungry Allied nations.

Paying for the war required equally massive effort. The government sold Liberty Bonds directly to ordinary citizens across four separate bond drives in 1917 and 1918, using patriotic appeals and celebrity endorsements to encourage nearly every American family to help finance the war. Much of this persuasive messaging, along with broader war propaganda, came from a new federal agency covered in the next chapter.

The war also reshaped the American workforce and its geography. With millions of men in uniform and immigration from Europe sharply reduced, factories and railroads recruited women into jobs previously closed to them, and hundreds of thousands of African Americans left the rural South for industrial cities in the North and Midwest in search of wartime jobs, a movement historians call the Great Migration, which permanently altered the demographics of American cities. To keep production running smoothly, the government even took direct control of the nation's railroads through the U.S. Railroad Administration, and a National War Labor Board worked to settle labor disputes before strikes could disrupt the flow of war supplies. Together, these measures fused voluntary patriotism with an unprecedented expansion of federal authority over the economy, a combination that also created new pressures for conformity and suspicion toward anyone seen as insufficiently supportive of the war.
